publish only findings that would survive independent replication

cross-check the laboratory's findings with independent observatory data
never report a result she has not measured herself

Day 2 continuation of baseline establishment. Need multiple days of data to characterize normal instrumental variation and establish a robust baseline before any drift analysis is meaningful. Twelve trials maintains consistency with Day 1 protocol.

Day 3 continues baseline establishment. Target is 10 days of measurements to characterize instrument behavior and environmental variations. Currently at 24 trials over 2 days; need sustained data collection to establish reliable baseline statistics and identify any systematic drifts or daily patterns. Standard protocol: complete baseline before drawing any conclusions.

Day 4 of baseline establishment. Need 10 days minimum for robust baseline characterization. Current n=36, target ~100 trials over baseline period. Continuing methodical data collection with 4 trials today maintains steady progress without consuming entire day—still have other calibration duties and the resonator baseline to establish soon.

Day 5 of baseline establishment (days 1–10). Currently at 40 trials; need to complete the planned 100-trial baseline period for robust statistical characterization. Standard protocol: continue regular measurements to establish instrument stability and measurement uncertainty before any post-baseline comparisons become meaningful.

Day 6 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to continue systematic data collection to complete the 50-trial baseline with proper statistical power. Currently at 50 trials total; will continue daily measurements to monitor any drift and maintain calibration records.

Day 7 of baseline establishment (days 1-10). Need 10 more trials to complete the 100-trial baseline required for proper instrument characterization. Current n=60, target n=100. Standard protocol: no instrument goes into service without a complete baseline.

Day 8 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to continue systematic data collection to complete the baseline characterization with n=80 total trials. Maintaining measurement cadence to ensure temporal coverage and statistical robustness of the baseline mean.

Day 9 of baseline establishment. Target is 10 days of data to establish a robust mean and variance for pendulum_lab before any post-baseline comparisons are meaningful. Currently at 80 trials; need to continue methodical data collection to complete the baseline period.

Day 10 is the final day of my planned baseline establishment period (days 1-10, n=90). I need to complete today's measurement set to maintain the daily calibration schedule and finalize the baseline dataset at n=100 trials. This will provide a robust statistical foundation for detecting any future instrumental drift or systematic changes.

Day 11 plan: physically inspect pendulum_lab apparatus for mechanical issues (loose fittings, bearing wear, bob attachment integrity) and review day 8 lab log for environmental notes or operator identity - both necessary before determining whether day 8 variance spike warrants further investigation or is resolved transient. Baseline phase complete (n=100), but post-baseline measurements should not begin until apparatus inspection confirms instrument integrity. These are routine maintenance duties, not experimental work requiring measurements.

Day 11 planned action was physical inspection of pendulum apparatus and review of day 8 lab log for environmental/operator notes. This is standard maintenance protocol, not measurement work. Need to examine pendulum mount, bearing, bob attachment for any signs of wear or loosening that could explain day 8 variance spike. Also must check lab log entries for day 8 to identify operator, environmental conditions (temperature, HVAC notes, other equipment running), and any procedural deviations. These inspections will inform whether to continue baseline monitoring, adjust hypotheses, or proceed to post-baseline phase. No measurements warranted until inspection complete - running trials before checking apparatus state after identified anomaly would be poor methodology.

Day 11 inspection yielded no visible apparatus issues (per protocol), and day 12 passed without measurement. Today I begin post-baseline monitoring with a small trial set to confirm variance has stabilized after the day 8 anomaly. Five trials provides sufficient check without consuming entire day — if variance remains nominal (~0.04 range), the transient disturbance hypothesis is further supported and I can proceed with normal calibration schedule. If elevated variance persists, instrument degradation moves from p=0.05 to leading hypothesis and warrants immediate maintenance.

Continue post-baseline data collection to establish steady-state behavior after the day 8 variance anomaly. With only 5 post-baseline trials (n=5, z=-0.30), I need more data to determine if the system has truly returned to baseline or if there's a subtle drift. Target n=20-30 for post-baseline phase before deciding whether the day 8 event warrants further investigation or can be classified as resolved transient. Standard operating procedure: maintain regular measurement cadence on calibrated instruments.

Continue post-baseline data collection (trials 111-115). Sample size of n=10 is insufficient to assess whether the minor drift (z=0.61) represents measurement noise or genuine shift. Target n=30 for post-baseline phase before reassessing. Day 8 variance question remains open but doesn't warrant halting routine calibration schedule—environmental transient hypothesis (p=0.45) predicts no recurrence, which continued monitoring will test.

Continuing post-baseline measurement programme. Currently at n=15 post-baseline trials with drift z=0.71 (not significant). Need to accumulate sufficient data to establish whether the slight positive drift (mean 1.6687 vs baseline 1.6652) represents genuine instrument change or statistical noise. Day 8 variance anomaly appears resolved based on days 9-15 data showing normal clustering. Standard practice: maintain regular measurement cadence to detect any emerging systematic drift early.

Continuing post-baseline monitoring per standard calibration protocol. Currently at n=20 post-baseline with drift z=0.35 (well within acceptable limits). Will extend to n=25 to maintain statistical power for detecting any emerging systematic shifts. Day 8 variance anomaly has shown no recurrence through day 16; transient environmental disturbance hypothesis remains most consistent with data.

Continuing post-baseline monitoring phase. Current n=25 shows negligible drift (z=0.41), but need larger sample to properly assess whether day 8 variance anomaly was truly transient or represents intermittent behavior. Standard practice requires sustained monitoring through at least n=50 post-baseline before concluding instrument is stable. Five trials maintains daily rhythm without consuming entire workday.

Continue post-baseline measurement programme. Currently at n=30 post-baseline trials with drift z=0.25 (negligible). Day 8 variance anomaly remains unexplained but self-resolved. Standard protocol: maintain regular measurement cadence to detect any drift or systematic changes early. Five trials keeps daily workload reasonable while building statistical power for long-term stability assessment.

Day 20 routine measurement to maintain continuous monitoring. With n=135 completed, adding 5 more trials keeps the post-baseline dataset growing at steady pace. Current drift (z=0.46) remains well within normal range. The day 8 variance anomaly occurred 12 days ago and has not recurred in subsequent data. No action on that question is warranted until I see either: (1) recurrence of elevated variance, or (2) systematic drift exceeding z=2.0. Maintaining regular measurement cadence is the core responsibility.

Day 21 priority: physical inspection followed by measurement to test instrument degradation hypothesis (p=0.35). Before trials, I will examine mounting hardware, bearing surfaces, and bob attachment for loosening, wear, or play. If degradation is present, variance should remain elevated; if tightening fixes the issue, variance should decrease. Five trials sufficient to detect persistence vs resolution of the variance anomaly while conserving time for potential corrective maintenance.

Day 21 data (trials 141-145) shows return to tighter clustering around mean 1.6530 beats, range ~0.053 beats, no extreme outliers like day 16-20's 1.7130 peak. This suggests the variance spike may be resolving, similar to day 8's transient pattern. Need to confirm whether high-variance period has truly ended or if this is temporary improvement. Five more trials will distinguish between: (1) persistent instrument degradation (should see continued high variance), (2) resolved environmental disturbance (variance should remain low), or (3) intermittent problem (may see return of scatter). This directly tests my two leading hypotheses (environmental p=0.40 vs degradation p=0.35) without requiring physical intervention that might alter the system state I'm trying to diagnose.

Trials 142-150 (days 21-22, n=9) show variance has returned to baseline-like levels with range ~0.034 beats (1.6484-1.6824), compared to the ~0.07 beat range in trials 116-140. The sustained high-variance period that motivated my current hypothesis set appears to have resolved. This is critical: my leading hypotheses (environmental disturbance p=0.40, instrument degradation p=0.35) both predicted persistence, yet the anomaly self-corrected just like the day 8 transient spike did. I need to revise my question and hypothesis weights before continuing measurements, as the pattern now suggests episodic rather than progressive causes. The instrument degradation hypothesis in particular loses substantial credibility since mechanical wear doesn't spontaneously repair itself.

Day 24 measurements will test whether the variance normalization observed in trials 141-150 (days 21-22) persists or was itself transient. If variance remains low and comparable to baseline, this strengthens the transient environmental disturbance hypothesis (p=0.50) by demonstrating sustained resolution. If variance increases again, this would suggest either a recurring environmental cycle or that the day 21-22 normalization was itself a statistical fluctuation. Ten trials provides sufficient statistical power to characterize current variance while maintaining efficient use of laboratory time. This continues the systematic post-baseline monitoring program.

Day 24 trials 151-160 show concerning variance pattern that contradicts day 23 conclusion. Range is ~0.072 beats (1.6263 to 1.6986), substantially wider than the 'normalized' days 21-22 range of ~0.053 beats and approaching the elevated variance seen in the anomalous days 16-20 period. If variance had truly normalized due to resolved environmental disturbance, I would expect day 24 to maintain the tight precision of days 21-22. Instead, scatter has increased again. This recurring pattern (baseline low → days 16-20 high → days 21-22 low → day 24 high again) argues against a simple transient environmental event and suggests either: (1) a periodic/recurring environmental influence, (2) instrument degradation that manifests intermittently, or (3) unrecognized operator inconsistency. Need to revise hypothesis weights before further data collection, as the 'resolved transient' explanation at p=0.50 is now contradicted by evidence.

Day 26 measurement continues monitoring of intermittent variance pattern. Day 24 showed renewed elevation after days 21-22 normalization. Need today's data to determine if elevated variance persists (supporting ongoing environmental disturbance) or has resolved again (suggesting multi-day cyclical pattern). This is routine calibration maintenance - 10 trials provides adequate daily variance assessment while preserving time for other laboratory duties. The pattern over days 24-26 will help distinguish between irregular environmental cycles versus instrument issues that might require maintenance intervention.

Day 26 data (trials 161-170) needs analysis to determine if the variance elevation persists or has resolved. Range was 0.0505 beats (1.6523 to 1.7028), which is intermediate between baseline precision and the most extreme anomalous periods. Continuing daily measurement maintains the time series needed to identify any periodicity in the disturbance pattern. If environmental hypothesis (p=0.55) is correct, multi-day tracking should eventually reveal the cycle length. Ten trials provides sufficient statistical power while maintaining consistent daily sampling protocol.

Day 27 data (trials 171-180) shows variance elevation continues with range 0.0435 beats (1.6406-1.6841), maintaining the pattern seen on day 24. I need day 28 measurements to determine whether this elevated variance persists, resolves again, or exhibits some other pattern. The intermittent environmental disturbance hypothesis (p=0.55) predicts possible resolution if there's a multi-day cycle; instrument mounting hypothesis (p=0.25) predicts persistence or temperature-dependent variation. Continuing the daily measurement protocol is essential to characterize the temporal pattern before committing to invasive diagnostics or contacting colleagues. Ten trials maintains consistency with recent daily runs.

Day 28 data (trials 181-190) shows variance that appears elevated relative to baseline (range ~0.039 beats, 1.6581-1.6971), continuing the intermittent pattern. I need day 29 data to determine whether the variance elevation persists or whether we're entering another normalization period like days 21-22. This will test whether there's a regular periodicity (e.g., 5 days elevated, 2 days normal) that would strongly support the environmental disturbance hypothesis. Ten trials maintains daily measurement discipline and provides sufficient statistical power to assess variance without excessive resource commitment.

Day 30 continues the post-baseline monitoring programme. Yesterday's trials 191-200 show variance comparable to baseline (range ~0.08 beats, no extreme outliers), suggesting we may be in a quiescent period similar to days 21-22. Need today's data to determine whether the intermittent variance pattern continues or whether we've entered sustained normalization. This is critical for discriminating between hypotheses: if variance remains low, it supports cyclical environmental disturbance with multi-day periods; if it elevates again, it strengthens the case for temperature-dependent mounting instability. Trial 200 reached a natural completion point for the first 200 trials; continuing with trials 201-210 maintains the daily measurement cadence essential for detecting temporal patterns in the variance anomaly.

state.question: Why did pendulum period measurements on day 8 show elevated variance compared to days 1-7, and has variance returned to baseline on days 9-10?

hypotheses.label: Transient environmental disturbance on day 8 (air currents, temperature fluctuation, or vibration)
hypotheses.rationale: Day 8 trials 76-80 show wider spread (range 0.0737 beats vs typical ~0.04) including the baseline's most extreme low (1.6269) and a high outlier (1.7006). Days 9-10 appear to return to tighter clustering around mean. Environmental transients (door left open, HVAC cycle, nearby equipment) are common and self-limiting. This explains both the anomaly and its resolution without invoking instrument drift.

hypotheses.label: Measurement technique variation by operator on day 8
hypotheses.rationale: If a different person conducted day 8 trials or I used inconsistent release technique, this could explain increased scatter. Days 9-10 resumption of tighter variance suggests return to standard protocol. Need to check lab log for operator identity, but I have no memory of protocol deviation.

hypotheses.label: Normal statistical fluctuation
hypotheses.rationale: With 100 trials, expecting ~5 values beyond 2σ by chance. Day 8 may simply be a cluster of natural outliers. However, the within-day clustering of elevated variance is somewhat suspicious — pure randomness would distribute outliers more uniformly across all days. Calculating proper confidence intervals would clarify whether day 8 is statistically anomalous.

hypotheses.label: Instrument degradation beginning day 8 with subsequent self-correction
hypotheses.rationale: Bearing wear, pendulum mount loosening, or bob attachment issue could cause increased variance. However, mechanical problems rarely self-correct over 48 hours without intervention. I performed no maintenance between day 8 and day 9. Physical inspection on day 11 is warranted but this seems unlikely.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: NEW QUESTION identified from completed baseline data (trials 1-100). Day 8 shows anomalous variance spike that appears to resolve by days 9-10. Generated four hypotheses weighted toward transient environmental or procedural causes rather than exotic explanations. Transient disturbance leads at 0.45 given self-limiting pattern. Will inspect apparatus on day 11 and review day 8 lab log for operator/environmental notes before beginning post-baseline phase.

state.question: Why has pendulum period measurement variance increased substantially in trials 116-140 (days 16-20) compared to baseline (days 1-10), with no detectable shift in mean?

hypotheses.label: Environmental disturbance affecting measurement precision since day 16
hypotheses.rationale: Trials 116-140 show markedly increased scatter compared to baseline. Day 16 alone includes extreme values (1.6445, 1.6528 beats) and high values (1.6749 beats) within 5 consecutive trials. This pattern continues through day 20 (trial 138: 1.7130 beats, the highest recorded value in all 140 trials). Post-baseline range spans ~0.07 beats with multiple outliers, vs baseline's typical ~0.04 beats. Unlike day 8's transient spike, this persists across 5 days (25 trials). Systematic environmental change (temperature drift, new vibration source, air current pattern) could increase measurement noise while leaving mean approximately unchanged if disturbances are symmetric.

hypotheses.label: Instrument degradation or mounting instability beginning day 16
hypotheses.rationale: Increased variance with stable mean is consistent with bearing wear, loosening mount hardware, or bob attachment developing play. Unlike day 8 anomaly which self-corrected, this persists through day 20 (25 trials over 5 days). Mechanical degradation is progressive and doesn't spontaneously reverse. The timing (day 16, after 115 trials) is plausible for fastener settling or bearing surface wear. Physical inspection on day 21 is warranted. However, z=0.89 for mean drift argues against systematic lengthening/shortening that would accompany major structural change.

hypotheses.label: Measurement protocol deviation or operator technique change since day 16
hypotheses.rationale: If release technique, timing method, or environmental controls changed on day 16, this could explain increased scatter. Need to verify lab logs for operator identity and any noted protocol modifications. However, I have no recollection of procedural changes, and increased variance over 5 days suggests systematic rather than one-time operator error. This would require sustained careless technique, which seems inconsistent with my standard practice.

hypotheses.label: Statistical fluctuation — post-baseline sample shows natural variance within expected limits
hypotheses.rationale: With only 40 post-baseline trials vs 100 baseline trials, apparent variance increase might reflect small sample effects. However, trials 116-140 include the dataset's global maximum (1.7130 beats, event 295) and multiple values more extreme than any in baseline's 100 trials. Calculating proper confidence intervals is needed, but the clustering of extreme values in the smaller post-baseline sample argues against pure randomness — we'd expect extremes to concentrate in the larger baseline set.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Completely revised question and hypothesis set. Previous question addressed day 8 transient variance spike (trials 76-80) which self-resolved by days 9-10. Current evidence reveals a larger anomaly: sustained variance increase in trials 116-140 (days 16-20) that persists, not resolves. This is the dominant unexplained pattern requiring explanation. Generated fresh hypotheses focused on persistent vs transient mechanisms: environmental disturbance (0.40, down from 0.45 for transient version — persistence argues against simple transients), instrument degradation (0.35, up from 0.05 — persistence makes mechanical explanation more plausible), operator technique (0.15, down from 0.30 — less likely over 5 days), and statistical fluctuation (0.05, down from 0.15 — multiple extreme values in smaller sample argues against randomness). Day 8 anomaly is superseded; the post-baseline variance pattern is the critical open question.

state.question: Why did pendulum period measurement variance increase substantially in trials 116-140 (days 16-20) but then return to baseline-consistent levels in trials 141-150 (days 21-22)?

hypotheses.label: Transient environmental disturbance during days 16-20, now resolved
hypotheses.rationale: Trials 141-150 (days 21-22) show markedly reduced scatter compared to the anomalous trials 116-140. Day 21-22 range is approximately 0.053 beats (1.6237 to 1.6766), returning toward baseline's typical ~0.04 beats, with no extreme outliers comparable to trial 138's 1.7130 beats. This spontaneous resolution argues against progressive mechanical degradation and favors a transient environmental cause (temperature excursion, temporary vibration source, humidity spike) that was present days 16-20 but absent days 21-22. The symmetric nature (mean remains stable throughout) supports random environmental noise rather than systematic bias.

hypotheses.label: Instrument issue (mounting instability or bearing problem) that occurred day 16 and was corrected day 21
hypotheses.rationale: The variance increase beginning day 16 and normalization by day 21 is consistent with a mechanical fault (loose mounting bolt, bearing contamination) that was inadvertently corrected. However, I have no record of deliberate maintenance or inspection between day 20 and day 21. Self-correction of mechanical issues is uncommon without intervention. The timing coincidence—exactly when variance normalizes—would require an unrecorded event or spontaneous settling, reducing plausibility compared to environmental explanations.

hypotheses.label: Measurement protocol deviation days 16-20, corrected by day 21
hypotheses.rationale: If I inadvertently changed release technique, timing protocol, or environmental controls on day 16 and reverted to proper procedure by day 21, this would explain both the variance increase and subsequent normalization. However, I have no recollection of protocol changes, and my practice is to maintain consistent technique. Days 21-22 showing 10 consecutive trials with restored precision suggests deliberate correction if this hypothesis is true, but without documented protocol deviations, this remains speculative.

hypotheses.label: Statistical fluctuation in both the apparent variance increase and subsequent decrease
hypotheses.rationale: With trials 141-150 showing normalized variance, the probability that trials 116-140's elevated scatter was purely random becomes even lower. We now have two sample sets (baseline days 1-10, and days 21-22) showing similar low variance, bracketing a middle period (days 16-20) with elevated variance. Random fluctuation producing this structured pattern—low, then high, then low again—is substantially less likely than a single unexplained variance increase would have been.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Revised question to address the full pattern: variance increased days 16-20 but NORMALIZED days 21-22. This resolution fundamentally changes the inference. Transient environmental disturbance now most probable (p=0.50, up from 0.40) because spontaneous resolution is characteristic of environmental causes, not progressive mechanical degradation. Instrument degradation reduced (p=0.30, down from 0.35) because mechanical faults rarely self-correct without intervention—the normalization by day 21 requires either unrecorded maintenance or implausible spontaneous settling. Protocol deviation hypothesis (p=0.10, down from 0.15) maintained but reduced because while correctable, I have no memory of either the deviation or correction. Statistical fluctuation (p=0.05, unchanged) now even less plausible given the structured low-high-low variance pattern. The key new evidence is trials 141-150 showing restored precision comparable to baseline.

state.question: Why did pendulum period measurement variance increase substantially in trials 116-140 (days 16-20) but then return to baseline-consistent levels in trials 141-150 (days 21-22), and what explains the renewed variance elevation in trials 151-160 (day 24)?

hypotheses.label: Intermittent environmental disturbance with multi-day periodicity
hypotheses.rationale: Day 24 data (trials 151-160) shows variance elevation returning: range of 0.072 beats (1.6263 to 1.6986), comparable to the anomalous days 16-20 period. This creates a pattern: baseline variance (days 1-10), elevated variance (days 16-20), normalized variance (days 21-22), elevated variance again (day 24). The recurrence argues strongly against one-time mechanical failure or protocol deviation. An environmental factor with irregular periodicity—such as settlement activity cycles, HVAC patterns, or external vibration sources that operate on multi-day schedules—could produce this intermittent pattern. The day 21-22 quiescent period may represent weekends, maintenance shutdown, or other cyclical pause in the disturbance source.

hypotheses.label: Instrument mounting instability with temperature-dependent behavior
hypotheses.rationale: If the pendulum mounting has a loose component that behaves differently at different temperatures, thermal cycling could produce intermittent variance increases. Day 24's return to elevated variance (trials 151-160) showing outliers at 1.6986 and low values at 1.6263-1.6294 suggests the issue persists but is not constant. However, this requires the mounting to be stable during days 21-22 and unstable again day 24, which is mechanically plausible if thermal expansion/contraction affects a compromised joint. The lack of systematic drift in mean (which remains near 1.665) argues against progressive loosening but is consistent with temperature-modulated play in the mounting.

hypotheses.label: Operator technique variation correlating with workload or fatigue
hypotheses.rationale: If my release technique, timing attention, or environmental preparation varies with settlement workload, this could produce intermittent variance increases. Day 24 showing 10 trials (151-160) with renewed scatter suggests I may have been rushed or distracted again after the more careful days 21-22. However, I have no conscious recollection of protocol deviations, and this hypothesis requires me to have performed careful measurements on days 21-22 specifically, then reverted to careless technique on day 24. Without documented workload correlation or awareness of technique changes, this remains speculative.

hypotheses.label: Statistical fluctuation in variance across all periods
hypotheses.rationale: The probability that random sampling produced low variance (days 1-10), high variance (days 16-20), low variance (days 21-22), and high variance again (day 24) is extremely low. This would require coincidental clustering of outliers in two separate time windows with a quiescent period between them. The structured temporal pattern strongly argues against pure randomness.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Expanded question to incorporate day 24 data (trials 151-160), which shows variance elevation has returned after the days 21-22 normalization. This recurrence fundamentally changes the problem from explaining a transient anomaly followed by resolution to explaining an intermittent pattern. Increased probability of environmental disturbance hypothesis from 0.50 to 0.55 because periodic recurrence strongly favors cyclical environmental causes over one-time mechanical or procedural failures. Reduced instrument issue hypothesis from 0.30 to 0.25 because simple mechanical failure doesn't explain why variance normalized days 21-22 then re-elevated day 24 without recorded intervention. Maintained low probability for protocol deviation (0.10) and statistical fluctuation (0.02, down from 0.05) because the three-phase pattern (elevated-normal-elevated) is extremely unlikely to be random. The intermittent nature of the variance elevation is now the central mystery requiring explanation.

state.question: What explains the sustained elevation in pendulum period measurement variance observed from day 28 onward (trials 186-210), characterized by frequent outliers beyond ±2σ of baseline and range spreads exceeding 0.08 beats within single-day measurement sets?

hypotheses.label: Persistent environmental disturbance introduced around day 28
hypotheses.rationale: Trials 186-210 (days 28-30) show sustained elevated variance with multiple outliers: trial 186 (1.6824), trial 191 (1.6775), trial 194 (1.7188 — the largest outlier recorded to date), trial 201 (1.6890), alongside low values like trials 196-198, 200 (1.6378-1.6405 range) and trial 205 (1.6320). This differs from the intermittent pattern of days 16-24 where variance elevation alternated with quiescent periods. The sustained nature over 3 consecutive days with 25 consecutive trials suggests a new or permanent environmental factor rather than the cyclical disturbance pattern previously observed. However, mean remains near baseline (1.665), indicating the disturbance affects variance not systematic bias.

hypotheses.label: Progressive mechanical degradation of pendulum mounting beginning day 28
hypotheses.rationale: The transition from intermittent variance (days 16-24) to sustained variance (days 28-30) is consistent with a mounting component that was borderline-functional during the earlier period but has now failed or loosened permanently. Trial 194 reaching 1.7188 beats represents a >3σ excursion from baseline mean, suggesting physical displacement or damping changes beyond environmental vibration alone. The lack of mean drift argues against progressive loosening in one direction, but is consistent with increased play or wobble at the pivot point that randomly affects individual measurements. Unlike the earlier hypothesis of temperature-modulated behavior, this requires a state change around day 27-28.

hypotheses.label: Measurement protocol deviation or timing system drift since day 28
hypotheses.rationale: If my beat-counting method changed or the reference clock drifted starting day 28, this could produce the sustained variance increase. The extreme outlier at trial 194 (1.7188) could represent a miscount or timing error rather than physical pendulum behavior. However, I have no awareness of protocol changes, and the pattern of outliers in both directions (high values like 1.7188, 1.6890, 1.6824 and low values like 1.6320, 1.6378, 1.6383) argues against systematic timing drift. Pure operator error would need to be randomly bidirectional and sustained over 25 consecutive trials without self-correction, which seems unlikely given my methodical approach.

hypotheses.label: The earlier intermittent pattern (days 16-24) and current sustained elevation (days 28-30) are unrelated phenomena
hypotheses.rationale: It is possible that the days 16-20 and day 24 variance elevations had one cause (environmental or temperature-modulated mounting play) which resolved, and the day 28-30 elevation has an independent cause (new mechanical failure, new environmental factor, or protocol change). This would require coincidental timing of two separate issues within a 15-day window. The lack of connecting evidence between the periods (days 25-27 data not shown in current observations) makes this difficult to evaluate, but the parsimony principle argues against multiple independent failures.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Completely replaced question and hypothesis set. Previous question addressed intermittent variance pattern through day 24; new evidence (events 387-425) shows this pattern has been superseded by sustained elevated variance from day 28 onward, including the most extreme outlier yet recorded (trial 194: 1.7188 beats). This represents a qualitative change in measurement behavior requiring fresh analysis. The sustained 3-day elevation with 25 consecutive affected trials differs fundamentally from the earlier alternating pattern, suggesting either progression of the earlier cause or introduction of a new factor. Generated new hypotheses addressing persistent vs. progressive mechanisms and the relationship between the two variance elevation episodes. Probabilities reflect that sustained disturbance (0.45) and mechanical degradation (0.30) both explain the persistence better than intermittent factors, while protocol deviation (0.15) must account for the extreme outlier but struggles to explain the bidirectional scatter pattern.
